reference_contexts: Cheesecake Factory (CAKE) Deep Dive Analysis Cheesecake Factory Inc. (ticker: CAKE) is a small-cap company that owns and operates a number of restaurant brands including The Cheesecake Factory, North Italia, Social Monk Asian Kitchen, Grand Lux Cafe, and a variety of small brands under the Fox Restaurant Concepts umbrella. With a market capitalization of just under $2 billion, they are roughly on the line between small-cap and mid-cap companies. They have mildly outperformed the S&P 500 since inception, but with significant variance, including periods of dramatic outperformance during economic expansions and then reverting closer to the mean around recessionary times: Chart Source: Y Charts Over the past 1-year, 3-year, and 5-year periods, they have underperformed despite doing quite well fundamentally, mainly due to declining valuations. This has drawn my attention over the past couple months. This year, the company made a strategically important acquisition which was initially punished by the market, but that I think provides significant long-term growth potential to the restaurant chain. I’ll discuss this acquisition in more detail later in this report. Company Overview As the company describes in their latest 10-K filing: The Cheesecake Factory restaurants strive to provide a distinctive, high-quality dining experience at moderate prices by offering an extensive, innovative and evolving menu in an upscale casual, high-energy setting with attentive, efficient and friendly service. As a result, The Cheesecake Factory restaurants appeal to a diverse customer base across a broad demographic range. Our extensive menu and strategic selection of locations enable us to compete for substantially all dining preferences and occasions, from the key lunch and dinner day parts to the mid-afternoon and late-night day parts, which are traditionally weaker times for most casual dining restaurants, as well as special occasion dining. The Cheesecake Factory restaurants are generally open seven days a week for lunch and dinner, and we offer additional menu items for weekend brunch. Most of Cheesecake Factory Inc’s restaurants, including their namesake The Cheesecake Factory chain, target the upscale casual market, meaning fancier than casual but not as fancy as fine dining. For example, here’s what their The Cheesecake Factory interiors look like: Source: Cheesecake Factory October 2019 Presentation The Cheesecake Factory locations tend to be large and very busy, especially during the late night when many other restaurants are winding down. They have extremely broad menus, more than most restaurants, including steak, chicken, burgers, seafood, pizza, pasta, sandwiches, salads, and so forth. I personally don’t like that; I prefer restaurants that have a narrow menu that they specialize in, and for example I think The Cheesecake Factory’s steaks are rather poor compared to a proper steakhouse. However, a broad menu seems to have been working well for The Cheesecake Factory, because a whole family or dining group can find something they like on the menu. Naturally, The Cheesecake Factory specializes in dessert, and gets 16% of sales from dessert, which is much higher than most restaurants. While much of their menu is not particularly special in my view, their desserts are broadly considered to be exceptional. I don’t even particularly like cheesecake but I still like theirs. Over the past several years, third-party app-based delivery providers have expanded the restaurant’s reach. In 2009 they received 9% of sales from delivery orders, but in 2018 it was up to 14%. This is also a competitive threat, though, because delivery food via third-party apps has lower margins than dine-in eating. The company has 202 The Cheesecake Factory locations in the United States and one in Canada that are company-operated. The management team believes that they can eventually expand to 300 locations in the United States and 10 in Canada. The closest location to my home is approximately 1 hour away, for example. The only location I have visited is in Florida whenever I visit family there (they love the restaurant and brought my attention to it). I have close friends that have visited multiple locations throughout the northeast USA. The company also has 24 locations that operate in Mexico, the Middle East, and China that are licensed to third-party operators, with the first one having opened in 2012. There are currently three licensee operators of those 24 locations. The biggest licensee by far is based in Kuwait and has 16 locations throughout multiple Middle East countries and rights/options to expand into eastern Europe. They also can expand into Egypt, which is a huge 100 million population market with a lot of potential. I was in Egypt during much of October visiting family, and malls and restaurants there (often developed operators from Gulf states like Kuwait) are absolutely booming, and many of them have American restaurant brands like Chili’s. I could easily see a bunch of The Cheesecake Factory locations sprinkled into the mix; they would fit right into the higher-end development complexes. Another licensee is based in Mexico, currently has four locations in Mexico, and has rights/options to expand elsewhere in Latin America. The third licensee is based in Hong Kong, with four locations in China, and has rights/options for multi-country Asian expansion. With company-operated restaurants, the company pays the upfront costs and receives an average 20-25% cash-on-cash return from those locations. For licensed locations, the company doesn’t require any capital expenditure. Instead, they receive development fees and ongoing royalty fees, and they have a team dedicated to helping the licensed operators create and operate the locations in line with the company’s standards. The company reports that each international licensed location adds about $0.01 to the stock’s overall EPS. The company has internally developed and deployed a small number of other restaurant chains, including Grand Lux Cafe, Social Monk Asian Kitchen, and RockSugar Southeast Asian Kitchen. Lastly, they now also have over 21 North Italia restaurant locations, and 48 diverse restaurants within their recently-acquired FRC brand that I’ll get into later in this report. user_input: How has The Cheesecake Factory demonstrated a focus on long-term growth and stability in its business operations?
reference: The Cheesecake Factory, under the leadership of CEO David Overton since its incorporation in 1992, emphasizes long-term profitable performance rather than short-term quarterly results. This is evidenced by their strategy to earn an average return on invested capital (ROIC) of over 15% per year, which they often achieve. The company maintains a strong management hierarchy with many executives having long tenures, contributing to its stability and focus on mature, profitable operations. Additionally, Cheesecake Factory Inc has historically maintained little or no long-term debt, providing exceptional balance sheet strength for a small company. Despite borrowing approximately $300 million recently to finance the acquisition of Fox Restaurant Concepts (FRC), they maintain a manageable debt/income ratio of about 2-3x. This strategic approach underscores their commitment to long-term growth and stability.
reference_contexts: the late 1970’s, her son David Overton started opening small The Cheesecake Factory restaurants, and incorporated the chain into a company in 1992. David Overton remains the CEO to this day, and has successfully led the company with a long-term focus since its inception. Many other top executives at the company have long tenures as well. This isn’t a company that focuses on short-term quarterly results, and instead clearly focuses on long-term profitable performance and retaining their management hierarchy for long tenures. Multiple studies show that mature/profitable companies that focus on earning high returns on invested capital (ROIC) statistically do quite well, and Overton’s company specifically looks to earn an average ROIC of over 15% per year, which they often achieve. This is evidence of a well-run operation, but with natural periods of weakness that align with recessions. Chart Source: Y Charts The Cheesecake Factory has a 3.7 out of 5 rating on Glassdoor.com, which puts it higher than most other large restaurant chains for employee satisfaction. P.F. Chang’s has a 3.3 rating, Chili’s has 3.4, Olive Garden has 3.5, and Outback Steakhouse has 3.6. A few companies have higher ratings, like Longhorn Steakhouse has 3.9, and privately-owned In-N-Out Burger has an astoundingly high 4.3. Fox Restaurant Concepts, which is now a subsidiary of the company, also has an unusually high rating of 4.1. Cheesecake Factory Inc has also been rated as one of Fortune’s Top 100 employers for the past six years in a row. The company has historically maintained little or no long term debt, which gives them exceptional balance sheet strength for a small company. During the most recent quarter, however, they borrowed approximately $300 million in debt in order to finance the acquisition of FRC, and they plan to gradually pay this down. Even with this increased leverage, they only have a debt/income ratio of about 2-3x. In comparison, Bloomin Brands (the parent company of Outback Steakhouse) has a debt/income ratio of over 8x, which is very high. They trade at lower valuations than Cheesecake Factory Inc but have a lot less balance sheet flexibility. Growth Plans and FRC Acquisition There was a small company called Fox Restaurant Concepts (“FRC” for short), founded by Sam Fox in 1998, that serves as an incubator/developer for new restaurant concepts. Sam Fox has developed a highly successful record of building out restaurant ideas and selling some of the mature ones to other funds or businesses. In 2016, Cheesecake Factory Inc invested into two of Fox’s mature restaurant concepts, North Italia and Flower Child. Recently, after this multi-year period of successful co-investment, the company was in talks to purchase those mature restaurant chains from Fox. However, they decided to go a step further, and in July 2019, they announced an agreement to acquire all of Fox Restaurant Concepts. They now own North Italia, Flower Child, and a variety of smaller concepts, as well as the incubator structure itself. Sam Fox will continue to lead FRC as an independent subsidiary of Cheesecake Factory Inc, operating as a restaurant concept incubator. North Italia operations will move from FRC’s HQ in Arizona to the Cheesecake Factory’s HQ in California, so that the company can begin scaling that chain up alongside The Cheesecake Factory. The rest of the smaller concepts will continue to be led by FRC in Arizona, with the option to scale the mature ones up over time as they become mature and proven enough. North Italia currently has 21 locations, and Cheesecake Factory Inc expects that they can scale the chain to about 200 in the United States. They have a streamlined Italian upscale casual menu with an extensive wine and cocktail selection, and alcohol sales account for over 30% of total sales (compared to only 12% for The Cheesecake Factory restaurants). Private dining is a more significant portion of their sales than most restaurant chains. These locations are very profitable, with a 35% cash-on-cash return according to the company. The company expects to increase the location count of The Cheesecake Factory by about 3% per year, while North Italia and various FRC locations are expected to increase by 20% per year or more. The company’s namesake brand is the mature cash-generator, while these other concepts are the growth drivers. I think this acquisition has great synergy. FRC and their North Italia brand bring diversification and significant growth potential. Cheesecake Factory Inc brings plenty of capital for more rapid expansion of Fox’s mature restaurant concepts, and provides logistics and other operational infrastructure to scale them up as well. Valuation Analysis Cheesecake Factory Inc’s stock is not “cheap” by most measures, but it is appropriately-valued in my view at a time when many stocks are overvalued. It has a better balance sheet and stronger performance than many other restaurant chains, which affords it a higher valuation by the market. However, it is currently at-or-below its historical average valuation levels based on most time periods due to a recent bout of weakness. The stock currently has a dividend yield of over 3.3%, and has grown the dividend each year since they started paying it in 2012. And here are their P/S and P/B ratios since inception: Chart Source: Y Charts 1-year earnings growth: 9.9% 3-year annualized earnings growth: -1.9% 5-year annualized earnings growth: 6.3% 10-year annualized earnings growth: 9.6% 15-year annualized earnings growth: 7.7% Analysts on average currently expect 7.4% annualized earnings growth during the two years from the end of 2019 through the end of 2021. The company targets 13-14% annual returns going forward with their current post-acquisition structure, based on this breakdown: Source: Cheesecake Factory October 2019 Presentation I’m going to go ahead and just downgrade their revenue growth estimate from 8% to 6% right from the start for valuation purposes. The company grew revenue at a 3.7% annualized rate over the past five years and an 4.0% annualized rate over the past ten years. Granted, the company now has more aggressive growth drivers post-acquisition, and they expect The Cheesecake Factory to drive about half of the growth in line with their historical figures (3-4%) while North Italia and FRC are expected to drive the other half of growth with a faster pace from their much smaller base, which gives a credible reason to believe in upcoming growth acceleration. However, I’ll believe 8% when I see it. That’s double their 5-year and 10-year growth rates. For now, let’s conservatively say about 6% growth going forward based on significant contribution from these new opportunities. I’d rather be happily surprised to the upside rather than disappointed to the downside. Next, the company factors in a 2.5% dividend yield, but due to lower valuations currently, it’s more like 3.3%. That’s not bad, compared to the S&P 500 average yield of around 1.8% these days. Lastly, the company expects to reduce its share count by 1.5% per year, and to pay down acquisition debt over time even though its balance sheet remains in solid shape. Total capital returns from dividends, buybacks, and debt reduction are expected to average 5.5% per year. With $2.65 expected EPS for the full-year 2019, this is my base case valuation model: At the current price of $43.22, this stock is reasonably valued for 10% expected long-term returns without factoring in valuation expansion, which I believe is better than the S&P 500 is prepared to deliver from current valuation levels. In addition, with a strong balance sheet, good management, and a proven business model, it’s not very risky, as long as it is part of a diversified portfolio. With a more bullish scenario of 8% growth and eventually selling the stock for a higher earnings multiple of 18, 13-14% long-term returns are indeed possible from today’s price point, but I would not use that as my base case. That’s the optimistic case. Margin improvement from North Italia‘s growth could also give a performance boost. The base case is pretty good, the downside risks are real but well-managed in my view, and the upside potential is very significant. Basically, this is an example of a stock that transitioned from a high-valuation growth stock into a more mature dividend-paying quality/value stock with a more modest growth rate. However, with the acquisition of FRC and the company’s plan to scale North Italia nationwide, the company has a realistic path to increase their growth rate again. Risks Industry Competition- Moderate Risk The primary risk for any restaurant stock is that it ceases to have the most relevant food and environment for changing consumer preferences. The restaurant industry is one of the most challenging, and it requires good management to keep a tight ship and to continually update the menu and environment in order to maintain strong customer traffic. The company updates their menu twice per year, including pricing changes, and in response to criticism about their large portion sizes, The Cheesecake Factory has introduced what they refer to as a SkinnyLicious menu subset that focuses on lower-calorie portions. With Cheesecake Factory Inc’s strong management team, and with the added diversification of North Italia and other brands within Fox Restaurant Concepts, I believe that the company is well-protected from some of the more negative scenarios that restaurants can face. However, it’s always a risk worth monitoring. Margin Pressure- Major Risk Cheesecake Factory’s international licensed locations offer high margins, but their company-operated locations, which represent the bulk of their revenue, have been under margin pressure. Labor costs have been increasing but the company has been slow to raise menu prices. Operating margins reached a peak of 8.8% in 2016 but are currently as low as 5.9%. The growth of North Italia, with its significant alcohol mix leading to 35% cash-on-cash return potential per location, may help to offset these margin pressures as that chain becomes a larger portion of the overall company. Executive Retention- Moderate Risk As previously described, Cheesecake Factory Inc has been well-managed by its co-founder, David Overton, since 1992. He is currently 73, which means he could potentially have a decade or more leading the company ahead of him, or could retire at any time. The company has a strong executive team with long tenures at the company, but losing a co-founder as its long-time CEO would bring about transition risk. In addition, Cheesecake Factory Inc recently acquired Fox Restaurant Concepts, which is reliant on Sam Fox’s expertise. Fox is now leading this segment as an independent subsidiary of Cheesecake Factory Inc, and he has a proven track record of successful restaurant concepts. If he were to leave the company, it would bring about significant transition risk for this smaller but promising segment of the overall company. Economic Cycle- Moderate Risk Restaurant sales are moderately affected by the economic cycle. People eat out less, and may choose less expensive options, during recessionary periods. The U.S. restaurant industry is healthy and growing, with about $55 billion in revenue per month: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed Industry-wide revenue grows by about 5% per year on average, but during the severe recession of 2008/2009, the year-over-year industry growth briefly dropped to about -2%: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed This doesn’t seem like much, but it can have a substantial impact on operating margins, which are only 5-8% for a company like Cheesecake Factory Inc. Their earnings per share dropped by over 20% during the 2008/2009 recession. For the full year 2018, the company’s earnings per share were already down 14% from their 2016 highs, and is what led to a significant part of the stock’s recent decline. This is a risk worth factoring into growth rates, and is one reason why I instantly knocked down the company’s 8% target revenue growth to a baseline estimate of 6%. Growing by 8% represents an ideal potential year, where the industry is great and the company executes its new growth strategy well. Any long-term growth period, however, needs to assume that a recession occurs somewhere in there, severely throwing off expected growth numbers for a year or two. Stock Market Selloff- Moderate Risk Regardless of economic and earnings performance, Cheesecake’s stock could easily be subject to a sell-off should the S&P 500 face a severe correction. This particular stock was less volatile than the S&P 500 during the 2001 recession, but far more volatile than the S&P 500 during the 2008/2009 recession, with an 80% draw down from its high point. As of today, the stock is already in a 35% draw down from its 2017 all-time high of over $64/share. Chart Source: Y Charts It’s not hard to model a pretty severe scenario. Earnings drop by 20-25%, the valuation on those earnings falls by 20-25%, and you temporarily have share prices cut in half from their previous highs. This is the kind of stock that I approach as though I want to own the company for its future cash flows and mostly ignore fluctuating stock prices. However, those fluctuating stock prices can give us attractive entry prices to increase our position, and if the stock price ever gets way ahead of fundamentals, we can trim the position. Tax Changes- Moderate Risk U.S. corporations are enjoying the lowest tax rates they’ve had in modern history. Due to the U.S. corporate tax cuts that were passed in 2017 and came into effect in 2018, Cheesecake Factory has sharply reduced tax rates. These tax cuts were not paid for by reduced government spending; they were merely additive to the U.S. deficit, which now stands at 5% of GDP and growing. It’s quite possible that future administrations will reverse these corporate tax cuts, which would negatively impact the net income of most U.S. companies including Cheesecake Factory Inc. Many U.S. investors believe that they are “globally diversified” if they own an index like the S&P 500 or other broad U.S. stock index, since this collection of 500 U.S. companies gets over 40% of total revenues from outside of the United States. However, all companies in the U.S. are subject to the same jurisdictional risk- that the federal government could raise taxes on them or perform other acts to the detriment of their shareholder returns. For that reason, it’s useful to have a truly global portfolio that includes stocks headquartered outside of the United States as well.

user_input: How does the St. Louis Fed contribute to the analysis of housing starts and job openings in the U.S. economy?
reference: The St. Louis Fed provides data that contributes to the analysis of housing starts and job openings in the U.S. economy. For housing starts, it supplies charts showing both seasonally-adjusted figures and non-seasonally-adjusted figures, which help explain variations such as those seen in December when weather conditions were unusually mild. Regarding job openings, the St. Louis Fed offers data that tracks the total amount of U.S. job openings, revealing trends like the decline from over 7.3 million to 6.8 million and its correlation with year-over-year percentage changes in real GDP.
reference_contexts: Enterprise Products Partners L.P. (EPD) Deep-Dive Analysis Published January 19, 2020 This issue takes a look at the status of the U.S. business cycle, makes a case for platinum, and then explores arguably the best-managed midstream company in the United States. U.S. Business Cycle Status The U.S. economy continues to show an inconclusive-but-slowing pattern for economic output, even as the stock market pushes to new highs. Housing Starts: Solid, but Over-Reported The most surprising number from this past week, reported on Friday, was that housing starts came in with a blockbuster number. They had a massive spike up, which was way above estimates and received quite a bit of attention: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed The reduction in interest rates over the past year has been helpful for the housing market. Thirty-year fixed mortgage rates had increased to cycle highs of about 5% in late 2018, but have since fallen back down to between 3.50% and 3.75% within the past several months, which makes a big difference for home affordability. This seems to be helping housing demand. However, digging into it a bit more, December’s big gain was mainly due to seasonal adjustments. The non-seasonally-adjusted figure was far less spectacular: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed December is usually the lowest month for housing starts, because it’s cold in many parts of the country and because it’s the holiday season. However, this December was among the warmest and least-snowy Decembers on record for most of the United States, meaning it was a much “less-bad” home-building month than a typical December. So, housing starts declined, but did not decline as much as they usually do in December, and thus the seasonally-adjusted figure was remarkably high. Job Openings: Not So Good It was also reported on Friday that the total amount of U.S. job openings fell from over 7.3 million to 6.8 million, which was well below expectations. The job openings metric is now in its deepest year-over-year percent decline of this business cycle. The year-over-year percentage change in job openings tracks very closely to year-over-year percentage change in real GDP. Real GDP is reported quarterly with a considerable lag (we’re still waiting on the Q4 2019 figure, for example, which will come out at the end of January and then will be subject to revisions for a while), while job openings is a monthly metric, and therefore it gives an information lead on what the GDP report might look like or where it’s potentially headed. Job openings is only one economic variable and thus what it says is not perfect, but what it does say isn’t good: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed Some analysts are still referring to this as a solid number because they are looking at in absolute terms rather than year-over-year change terms, and the latter is more sensitive and informative of the two ways of organizing it. In absolute terms, the 6.8 million number of job openings remains high, and remains above the number of people who are officially unemployed. However, there is a skill/education/salary mismatch between job openings and people looking for work. Most economic indicators look great in absolute terms at this point in the economic cycle (earnings, employment, spending, etc). The moments that matter are when they start to fall from those great levels, which is why viewing the numbers in year-over-year percent change terms is usually more informative.

Kinder Morgan was considered the blue chip version of a master limited partnership; the long-standing gold standard of its industry. They built extensive pipelines throughout the United States, and funded that growth by issuing new units and by using high levels of debt leverage. For a very long time, this was a market-beating strategy with an amazing combo of yield and growth. But when oil prices crashed in 2015, the industry ran into a serious problem and MLP valuations fell dramatically. For a normal corporation, this would not have been as big of a deal. But because Kinder Morgan was reliant on continually issuing new shares to fund growth, and its share prices were suddenly cut in half, it quickly fell into a liquidity trap by losing its usual source of new capital. And because they were already highly leveraged, they couldn’t take on too much new debt. As a result, they had to cut the dividend and sell some of their assets at bad prices to raise liquidity and remain solvent, and years later they are still recovering. EPD avoided that problem by not having excessive leverage; they were able to operate normally and let their unit price recover before issuing more units for further growth projects. They used a mild increase in debt to get through that harder period, which they have since reduced. Now, many midstream companies including KMI and EPD have shifted towards a self-funding model. This means that they have purposely slowed down their distribution growth (or cut them in the case of KMI and many others) to create a larger source of inside capital. reference: Saudi Arabia's strategy regarding oil production has significantly impacted global economic conditions, especially during volatile market periods. Historically, Saudi Arabia attempted to oversupply the world with oil between 2014 and 2016 in an effort to bankrupt U.S. shale oil companies and reclaim market share. This strategy did not succeed as planned, leading Saudi Arabia to cut supply to raise prices instead. Recently, amid declining demand due to the coronavirus pandemic and China's economic shutdown, Saudi Arabia and Russia declined to reach a deal to cut oil production. Instead, they decided to increase oil supply in a coordinated effort to maximize market share by bankrupting higher-cost or indebted producers worldwide. This strategy has resulted in a historic drop in oil prices, with oil falling over 20% in one day alone and about 50% from the start of the year, pushing many producers into unprofitable territory. The low oil price environment is particularly damaging to U.S. shale oil producers with high ongoing production costs, as it becomes unprofitable for them to produce new marginal barrels once their hedges wear off. This situation has exacerbated global economic conditions during a period already marked by significant market volatility.
reference_contexts: A Historic Day for Updates Published March 9, 2020 With market volatility so high, I’m publishing more of these unscheduled notes than scheduled reports these days. I also have a new article out on Seeking Alpha regarding current debt-laden economic conditions. Today was one of the largest declines in the S&P 500 and Dow Jones history in percent terms, and is reminding investors everywhere that equity markets have real risk. It is times like this that I begin, carefully, putting capital to work. Specifically, it’s the fourth-ever largest percent daily drop for the Dow in post-WWII history, and one of the top ten S&P 500 drops in that timeframe as well. And during the day, the S&P 500 triggered a stock market circuit breaker and was shut off for 15 minutes. Treasuries and precious metals continue to hold up quite well as defense, while global equity markets are a mess. The S&P 500 is down almost 19% from its all time high, or a little more than 1% shy of entering arbitrary “bear market territory”, which is generally thought of as 20% down from all-time highs. Here’s how this drawdown compares to other drawdowns since roughly WWII: Futures are currently pointing towards a positive open tomorrow, but that can change overnight. After a day down this hard, it’s normal to have both volatile up and down days for a while. The Oil War And if you thought the stock move today was unusual, the oil price crash was truly historic. Oil fell over 20% today alone, is down about 50% from where it started the year, and is now deeply in unprofitable territory for the vast majority of worldwide producers. Due to the coronavirus, and particularly China’s economic quarantine/shutdown during the past month, oil demand has diminished this year. Normally the group of oil-producing nations that collectively make up OPEC, along with their partnership with Russia, would cut oil production to preserve higher oil prices, to balance supply with demand. However, U.S. shale oil has been growing and taking market share from them for the past decade. During the 2014-2016 period, Saudi Arabia purposely tried to oversupply the world with oil to bankrupt U.S. shale oil companies and take back market share, but it didn’t quite work and Saudi Arabia ended up relenting and cutting supply to raise prices, and thus forfeit market share. During the past week, Russia and Saudi Arabia declined to reach a deal to cut oil production. Going a step further, both of them instead decided to increase oil supply. This is attempt #2 to take back market share, this time more coordinated. It is the perfect storm for the energy market, and a truly historic moment, because oil demand is weak and oil supply will now be maximized. This is a scorched-earth attempt to take market share back by bankrupting many higher-cost or indebted producers worldwide, and is particularly damaging to the weaker half of U.S. shale oil producers. There are many different types of oil, with different cost structures. Investors often focus too much on the total cost of a barrel of oil to produce, rather than the more detailed cost breakdown. Some types of oil, such as Russian production, has big upfront costs but then rather low marginal costs after that, with big reserves. Other types of oil, like shale, have small upfront costs but then rather high marginal costs after that, with small reserves. And then companies all have different levels of balance sheet strength to get through hard times. This low oil price environment is bad for all oil producers, but is a deathblow to that second type of group that has high ongoing production costs, because after the oil companies’ hedges wear off, it’s unprofitable to produce every new marginal barrel. They are the ones that will have a tough time surviving, and many will go bankrupt if this continues for a while. The first type of oil producer, the kind that already made a big upfront investment and now has low-cost operational production, can weather the storm better and come out the other side. For both groups, a strong balance sheet and the amount of hedging they had in place both help their survival odds.

user_input: How has the coronavirus accelerated market volatility and impacted economic indicators according to recent analyses?
reference: The coronavirus has significantly accelerated market volatility, leading to a historic week in global stock market history with volatility levels comparable to those of 2008, 1987, or 1929. The pandemic's impact was unexpected and faster than anticipated, exacerbating existing economic issues such as flat corporate profit growth in 2019 and rising U.S. government deficits. Many year-over-year economic indicators were already pointing flat or down before the virus hit. Additionally, debt levels are near record highs globally, with varying financial stability across different regions. The coronavirus has tested the global financial system by affecting sectors like tourism heavily reliant on international visitors, as seen in Thailand's case, and U.S. restaurants facing unprecedented declines in sales. This situation is likely to lead to a recession similar to 2007, characterized by high government debt, consumer credit, and corporate debt levels, while mortgage debt remains lower than before.
reference_contexts: Market Crash Deep Dive Analysis Published March 15, 2020 This past week has been one of the most historic weeks in global stock market history, on par in terms of volatility with 2008, 1987, or 1929. Rather than do a deep dive on an individual stock as usual, this report’s deep dive will be on the whole macro situation along with several stock examples, due to the unprecedented market situation. Nobody has the full picture including me, and in this environment anything can happen, but a lot of the things we’ve been tracking for a couple years now, in my free newsletters and articles, and more recently in this premium research service, are coming home to roost and these are key turning points to see how they turn out. The main surprise is that it’s all happening faster than expected, accelerated by the coronavirus and more specifically the quarantine response to it. There’s often a curve ball or black swan somewhere, and this time it was a virus. Many pundits on CNBC and other media outlets seem to think that the economy was doing just fine before this hit, but that was not the case. Corporate profit growth was 0% in 2019, and excluding buybacks and tax cuts has been flat for several years before the involvement of trade wars or viruses. Most year-over-year economic indicators were pointing flat or down. Debt levels are near record highs, and the bottom half of the U.S. population is deeply financially insecure, more than they have been historically. The U.S. government deficit as a percentage of GDP has been rising dramatically since 2016; it’s supposed to shrink during a strong economy. Europe and Japan are better or worse in some ways, with even higher total debt levels but more financially secure people in the lower income levels. Germany has had a government budget surplus from which it can now draw from. With emerging markets, it varies significantly depending on the specific nation. Some are financially stable, like Taiwan or Thailand, while others like Argentina, Indonesia, and Mexico are more troubled. This situation will put the global financial system to the test in ways we saw coming, and in ways we won’t. For example, Thailand is in financially good shape with large financial reserves, but is heavily reliant on $60+ billion/year in tourism revenue, which is drying up from this virus more than it would in a normal recession. Many U.S. restaurants are in decent shape financially, but can they handle months with limited customers, in a far deeper restaurant sales decline than a normal recession? We’ll see. The Systemic Debt Issue The United States reached a peak total debt (public + private) at 380% of GDP in 2009. That was our all-time record high. More specifically, the U.S. entered that recession with a total debt/GDP ratio of a bit under 350%, and it grew to 380% during the process. After a period of modest deleveraging, mainly in the housing sector, we’re currently back down to just under 350% debt to GDP. So, we’re entering this likely recession with a similar level of debt as 2007. Specifically, we have way higher government debt, as well as higher consumer credit and corporate debt, but lower mortgage debt compared to that time, as a percentage of GDP. The third highest debt level ever reached was back in the Great Depression that started in 1929. In the early 1930’s at its peak, we reached 300% debt to GDP. It’s too far back to be on the St. Louis Fed chart above, but there are other data sources that recorded it. In fourth place was the 2001 recession, which was entered with about 275% debt to GDP. Debt magnifies everything, and is a big variable for what makes some recessions worse than others. The Great Depression of 1929 and the Great Recession of 2008 were so severe in part because debt levels were so historically high. Those two periods are “special” in terms of how rapidly the monetary base was expanded to deal with them compared to every other recession. This is a chart of the U.S. monetary base in log form, so every move up is exponential and this makes it easier to see the differences between normal exponential growth and accelerated exponential growth. Those periods from 1930-1950 and 2008-present represent multi-fold increases in the monetary base in a short period of time, while every other recession on the chart looks normal. The zero bound on interest rates was hit in these two major periods, so they just printed money for stimulus instead, roughly speaking. A few years after the initial 1929 crash, the U.S. devalued the dollar and began printing money from 1932 and onward to fund various programs. Then it slowed down, and in 1937 they encountered another recession, which was still within the larger context of the Great Depression period. So they turned on the printing presses again, and kept them on all through WW2. We’re most likely about to mirror that period in the 2020’s in terms of monetary policy (hopefully without the war part). The Great Recession triggered several rounds of exponential monetary base expansion from 2008 to 2014, and then they stopped until 2019. During this next period, we’re about to have another big increase in the monetary base, similar to what happened in 1937. We already started in September 2019 when the repo spike happened and the Fed started monetizing Treasury bills, and it’s likely about to get amplified.

user_input: How are airlines affected by the current economic conditions as described in the context?
reference: Airlines are among the industries that will be hit by economic shutdowns due to their high levels of debt. Many businesses, including airlines, are drawing on their revolving credit facilities from banks to pull extra cash onto their balance sheets to deal with upcoming challenges.
reference_contexts: The Banking Sector Back in 2008, banks themselves were undercapitalized, so they crashed harder than the broader economy. It’s the opposite this time; U.S. banks are quite well capitalized with plenty of reserves due to all the changes since 2008. However, the broader corporate sector is highly indebted and many industries will be hit by economic shutdowns (airlines, hotels, oil producers, restaurant chains, movie theaters, malls, concert venues, anything tourism related, etc). Tons of businesses are already drawing on their revolving credit facilities from banks, meaning they are pulling extra cash from banks onto their balance sheets to deal with whatever comes next. Some obvious companies like Boeing and Hyatt are raising cash, but even companies with strong balance sheets and plenty of cash already like Micron (a big RAM/NAND semiconductor producer) are tapping into their facilities to maximize cash levels even further. This puts a lot of pressure on the banking system. Just like how banks are not designed to hand out cash deposits to all of their customers at once, they are not designed to fulfill all of their client revolving credit facilities at once. The FRA/OIS spread, which is a measure of interbank liquidity, spiked this past week to levels not seen since 2008, meaning there is a serious liquidity problem. The Fed initially tried to address this liquidity problem, along with the liquidity problem that was happening in the Treasury market (which really is all part of the same issue) by announcing literally trillions of dollars in open repo lending lines going forward, which is the biggest ever such move, but that didn’t work at all. Banks only borrowed a small portion of that, roughly $100 billion, despite their rising liquidity problems. This seems to have to do with regulations; repo liquidity (which is borrowed rather than permanent) is not going to cut it. The dollar index started to spike and was briefly relieved when the Fed announced that liquidity bazooka, but it was temporary relief for about a day as market participants realized that it didn’t work and that it never entered the system. After that failed, the Fed outright bought $33 billion in Treasuries in one day on Friday, which served as a permanent liquidity injection, but only a small one compared to what is happening. Here’s how the dollar index responded this week, pretty much down to the hour: As I wrote the above content on Saturday and Sunday, the Federal Reserve just announced Sunday evening that they’ll cut interest rates to zero and initiate a massive $700 billion asset purchase program (“QE”). This will include $500 billion in Treasury purchases and $200 billion in mortgage-backed securities purchases. And it’ll be front-loaded; they’ll start with $40 billion all in one day on Monday. This is a pure permanent liquidity injection at a very large scale. In other words, they just dropped a $700 billion liquidity nuke, after their liquidity bazooka misfired last week. This is shaping up to be the key moment that the dollar bulls and dollar bears have been debating over for years now, and I have an article about the global dollar shortage that provides context on the background for it. The dollar’s value relative to other major currencies sharply dropped during the stock market crash starting 3 weeks ago, but when this liquidity issue started to show up this past week and the Fed’s initial attempt to provide massive liquidity failed, the dollar began spiking back up. Here’s a zoomed-out view of the dollar index in recent months: Towards the right of the chart there is a sharp deflationary crunch and an acute liquidity problem. That type of volatility between major currencies is highly unusual. However, now that the Fed just announced a cut to zero and a massive asset purchase program, it should weigh on the dollar in the week ahead. On one hand there’s an acute liquidity shortage pushing the dollar up, and combating that is the Fed’s massive liquidity injection, and we’ll see which force is more powerful in the near term.

user_input: What happnd to APMEX during high volatilty in metal markets?
reference: During periods of extreme volatility in the precious metals market, large dealers like APMEX experienced record physical metal buying. Due to this surge in demand, they posted notices on their websites about long shipping delays and higher minimum orders. reference_contexts: The Precious Metal Divergence As I said in the previous report, volatility of this extreme level shakes the financial system down to its very foundations and tests securities across the board. In addition to stocks and corporate bonds selling off, safer havens like Treasury bonds and precious metals were hit this week, and several ETFs experienced record high dislocations, meaning that the difference between their market price and their net asset value (the sum value of all the stocks or assets they hold) reached a record large divide. For example, suppose there is an ETF that holds one share of Apple and one share of Amazon for each share of the ETF. You would expect the ETF’s efficient market price to be equal to the sum of Apple and Amazon’s share prices (which is the net asset value), or at least within a penny or so. Ninety-nine percent of the time, that’s the case. During extreme market events, however, with Apple and Amazon shares rising or falling by double-digit percentage points every day, that divide between market price and net asset value can widen. That’s the type of thing that happened to several ETFs this week, except the ETFs have dozens or hundreds of positions rather than just two as in this example. It appears that a number of risk parity funds had to unwind their positions. Risk parity funds invest in both stocks and bonds with heavy leverage. When stocks go down, bonds usually go up, which helps cushion the blow and keeps overall volatility low. This week, however, Treasury bond yields increased sharply, meaning that Treasury bond prices dropped sharply. The TLT 20+ year Treasury ETF, for example, dropped by nearly 15% from its sharp peak in just a few days: That’s not normal bond behavior. With Treasuries crashing so swiftly alongside stocks, leveraged funds holding stocks and bonds were in trouble and some probably liquidated, which results in indiscriminate selling. With yields going back up while there’s a deflationary crunch, it can put downward pressure on gold and silver temporarily as well. Late last week, and especially on Friday, gold, silver, platinum, and in particular palladium all sold off sharply. It was one of the record high volatility days for the whole metals complex. The move in the GDX gold miner’s ETF was particularly fascinating. It sold off so sharply on Thursday that it reached a -4% divergence from its net asset value, which was an all-time record. Then on Friday it broke that record by going to a -7% divergence from net asset value. Basically, there was so much indiscriminate selling pressure on GDX that market makers didn’t have time to arbitrage the discount to net asset value. This means that GDX’s market price closed Friday at over 7% below the sum value of the shares of gold miners it holds. President Trump gave a speech at around 3:30pm on Friday, where he declared a national emergency, which potentially opens the floodgates for federal bailout money to help states and businesses deal with the coronavirus shutdown. Stocks were already up for the day before then, but went sharply vertical upward during the speech to become one of the best S&P 500 days in market history. At the same time, gold miners went sharply down with ever-faster acceleration, before snapping furiously back up right into the final minutes of the trading day, and then were up sharply in after-hours trading. The last time that GDX had such a sharp sell-off was in 2008, shortly before it exploded higher. I don’t know what will happen going forward, but this has all the hallmarks of an indiscriminate selling liquidity crunch. Some big fund may have been long gold miners and short the S&P 500, and sharply unwound the position when the S&P 500 started to rally during the speech. Whatever exactly happened, something big liquidated or squeezed or broke. I bought some GDX right at the bottom there and updated it in real time in the Google Drive, but it all happened so fast, within minutes. What makes the sell-off in precious metals and miners even more interesting, was that at the same time it was happening, precious metal physical dealers were experiencing record physical metal buying. Large dealers like APMEX, JM Bullion, and many others put notices on their websites saying that due to extreme order volume, there would be long shipping delays, higher minimum orders, and so forth. We wanted to provide our customers with important updates about our company, including a new temporary $299 minimum order, as well as the overall state of the industry. Over the last few weeks, we have seen record order volume, with yesterday being our largest sales day of all time. We are on pace for another record day today. As a business, we are doing everything we can to keep up, but with a 3-5x increase in order volume, we are unable to answer our phones and ship orders as quickly as usual. You can expect temporary shipping delays of 5-10+ business days while we scale up our operations to satisfy this unprecedented level of demand. -JM Bullion The U.S. Mint sent out a note to its authorized dealers saying that they were out of stock on American silver eagle coins due to excessive sales volume: This is to inform you that we have temporarily sold out of American Eagle silver eagle bullions. Our rate of sale in just the first part of March exceeds 300% of what was sold last month. West Point is working diligently to produce additional inventory and once additional inventory is produced, we will again begin allocations. -U.S. Mint This divergence between the physical market and the paper market can only last for a finite time, and will resolve in one direction or the other. If it stays like this, it means there’s a shortage, and physical metals will start getting a wider premium over the paper price until the paper price responds. Precious metals

user_input: Johnathan Taylor, how do foreign-exchange reserves relate to a country's ability to support its currency strength and manage external debt obligations?
reference: Reserves as a % of GDP are important for supporting a country's currency strength and backstopping external debt obligations when necessary. This metric is particularly crucial for emerging markets but is relevant for all markets.
reference_contexts: Reserves as a % of GDP: Different countries have very different levels of foreign-exchange reserves when it comes to supporting their currency strength and backstopping external debt obligations when necessary. This is a more important metric for emerging markets but is relevant for all markets. Trade and trade balances as a % of GDP: Some countries are more reliant on exports/trade than other nations. And apart from that, some countries have trade surpluses while others have trade deficits, which is important when measuring how overvalued/undervalued a currency is and how competitive a market is on a global basis. Net International Investment Position as a % of GDP: A country that owns more foreign assets than foreigners own of their assets is a creditor nation (such as Japan). A country that owns fewer foreign assets than foreigners own of their assets is a debtor nation (such as the United States). For example, the United States and its citizens/firms (mainly its citizens/firms) own $29 trillion in foreign assets (stocks, bonds, and real estate), while foreigners own $40 trillion of U.S. assets, which gives the U.S. an -$11 trillion net international investment position, or about -52% of U.S. 2019 GDP. The United States became a creditor nation after World War I, meaning it owned more foreign assets than foreigners owned of its assets. However, by 1985, an accumulation of trade deficits left the United States to become a debtor nation. We kept consuming more than we produced, which means we sent dollars abroad each year and foreigners used those dollars to buy American assets. Meanwhile, Japan produced more than they consumed, so they accumulated dollars and other currencies, and used them to buy American assets and other foreign assets, which made them a creditor nation. During the 2008 crisis, the United States had a NIIP of about -10% of GDP. Since then, it has deteriorated to worse than -50% of GDP by 2019. It would require a current account surplus (and likely a weaker dollar relative to other currencies) to begin reversing that trend. On one hand, we have a generationally large amount of debt in the system, and the system was hit by the external shock of the pandemic. On the other hand, we have the counterforce of extreme fiscal stimulus pushing back against that. As such, the relative flow of that tug-of-war impacts the inflation/deflation trade as well as most risk assets broadly. Whether a given company performs strongly or weakly in this year or next, is more dependent on fiscal policy and other macro forces than in a normal year, because those fiscal policy decisions affect the solvency of their customers in a broad sense. Other assets like gold, silver, and Bitcoin have followed the same basic pattern: crashing in March, surging into August, and then beginning to roll over, roughly in line with the inflation trend shift or in some cases front-running it a bit. In other words, as the Treasury market shifted its expectations from a rebound in inflation to a cooling off of inflation, risk assets and inflation hedges across the board have pulled back. Back in March, virtually all asset classes other than cash and T-bills were crashing (even briefly T-bonds were falling at the worst part of the liquidity event), and a deflationary view was forming in the market. Congress got serious about passing a multi-trillion-dollar fiscal emergency bill, inflation expectations bottomed on March 19, the stock market bottomed on March 23, and the CARES Act was passed on March 27. This was followed by several months of sharp upward moves in the prices of most asset classes, against the backdrop of rapid broad money supply increases, deeper and deeper negative real yields, fast central bank balance sheet growth, and a weakening dollar. In other words, it was a direct fiscal stimulus into the economy, monetized in large part by the Federal Reserve. From April through July, people received stimulus checks and extra unemployment benefits, and small businesses received loans that turn into grants, nearly $3 trillion in free grant money overall, but most of that stopped by the end of July. Some of it happened with a lag; unemployment benefits attributed to previous weeks still went out to people into mid-August. Now, at the end of August, the economy has been operating for a couple weeks in “non-fiscal” mode. Unemployed people are not receiving additional federal unemployment benefits, and businesses are pretty much on their own. Small business revenue peaked in the beginning of July and has since been on a downtrend. July consumer confidence reached a new cycle low after enjoying a brief bounce. If this situation continues with high unemployment and low government stimulus, the natural results of a major recession will play out, with many people and businesses unable to pay rent, which trickles up to landlords and banks, and results in a broad solvency crisis and many defaults. So far, national personal income was up in 2020 (rather than down as in a normal recession), due to increased government transfer payments that more than offset the loss of normal income. And that led to retail sales also being up in 2020 (largely lead by e-commerce), because consumers have that government cash to spend, even as employment conditions, imports, exports, industrial production, and capital spending are all down as per what we’d expect from a severe recession. That divergence between incomes going up and economic activity going down is not inherently sustainable, unless government spending artificially continues to sustain it. Both political parties want another round of stimulus. The Republicans and President want about $1 trillion in stimulus, mainly targeting businesses and consumer stimulus checks again. The Democrats want $3 trillion in stimulus, targeting state budgets and larger consumer stimulus checks this time. Both sides have signaled compromise; Democrats are willing to go down to $2 trillion, and Trump is willing to go up to $1.3 trillion. Political events related to the upcoming election and unrelated to stimulus, largely involving the Post Office, have further slowed down these negotiations. The situation remains in gridlock, and so the economy has gone off the “fiscal cliff”. Analysts don’t expect S&P 500 earnings and revenue to surpass 2019 highs until 2022, even though the stock market has already reached new record highs in 2020, due to increases in valuation. As long as that fiscal gridlock remains, a disinflationary pressure and broad solvency risks grow. The Fed’s balance sheet stopped increasing nearly three months ago. Broad money supply stopped increasing about a month ago. The stock market and consumer finances are no longer held up by “money printing” at this particular time. Equities and other risk assets, which have kept going up, are vulnerable for correction in this environment. -August 30 deep dive report In essence, whenever the backdrop involves massive fiscal spending, rising inflation expectations, negative real interest rates that are becoming more deeply negative, and rapid increases in broad money supply; the logical move is to be in scarce assets. This includes things like precious metals, commodities, good-quality stocks, and Bitcoin, depending on your preferences. However, when the backdrop turns into gridlock and lack of fiscal stimulus, falling inflation expectations, rising real yields, and slower broad money supply growth, a more defensive position that includes cash and T-bills makes sense, potentially with hedges in place against drops in risk assets depending on what type of portfolio you run. We’re in a defense/disinflation environment until signs of stimulus emerge. On one hand they are getting a bit closer, with the Democrat-controlled House of Representative currently drafting a $2.4 trillion spending bill that is closer in size and scope to what the Republicans have said they would support. On the other side, the Republicans have moved up their target to $1.5 trillion, so the numbers are starting to converge towards the middle of maybe $2 trillion. I’ll leave the probability assessment of stimulus happening prior to the election to political specialists, and instead just watch the debate play out. This is due to operational leverage where fixed expenses remain constant while variable income decreases. So, specific regulations that enforce data privacy and reduce the ability of Facebook to target ads to users, would reduce the effectiveness of Facebook ads, and therefore reduce their returns on invested capital and their overall profit margins and growth rate. And the result is nonlinear due to operational leverage: fixed expenses vs variable income. By rough calculations, if their ads were 25% less profitable but the company’s expenses were the same, it would be in the ballpark of a 40-50% profit reduction. If their ads were 50% less profitable, the company would have approximately zero profit. Cultural Backlash After the Cambridge Analytica data scandal, #DeleteFacebook became a popular movement. Like many movements, it didn’t really go anywhere. Facebook’s reputation was tarnished a bit, some advertisers pulled out, but their users and revenue keep going up around the world. Notably, the movement didn’t really include Instagram or WhatsApp. I deleted my Facebook account back before it was “cool” to do so, years ago. Twitter is the only broad social media platform I personally use, since it is popular among investors. Anti-Trust Risk The past couple decades have been an era of loose anti-trust activity by historical standards. We have an unusually large degree of consolidation of platforms into a handful of mega-corporations. A collection of growth companies can work well if you spread out your bets by a reasonable degree. From the company side, Facebook has $58 billion in cash and no long-term debt, which gives them remarkable flexibility to change and adapt as needed to keep their business model relevant, and in line with shifting regulator and cultural standards. Lastly, Facebook as I previously pointed out, has about 90% of their users outside of the United States. They operate in jurisdictions around the world. AI Cybersecurity Risks Ramping Up There is a growing divide between closed-weight and open-weight AI models. Closed-weight models such as Claude and ChatGPT are typically developed by the leading labs, are the most advanced, and the user has no control over them. To use them, the user connects with the provider’s server. The provider can restrict access, block certain queries, and see all the personal or business secrets that the user hands over as part of their AI usage. Open-weight models (which are almost all Chinese now) are several months behind the leading labs’ closed weight models in terms of capability at any given time, but much like open-source software, they come with a lot of advantages. The user can download them and run them on their own machine (or many other third parties can run it for users on their servers as a service), which means privacy for the user and lack of control by the producer. They can additionally be evaluated and fine-tuned by the user. As a result, open-weight models have been sharply gaining market share here in 2026. Advocates for closed-weight models often argue that it’s dangerous for open-weight models to exist. They view AI as extremely powerful and thus it must be controlled. And of course, the leading labs are worth about a trillion dollars in market cap and don’t enjoy having countless open-weight competitors. Advocates for open-weight models generally argue that it’s inevitable (there’s no way to take down code globally), and it broadens access to AI rather than forming regulatory moats around a small group of AI corporations to protect them from competition. Here’s the topical problem: Both closed-weight and open-weight models, when they produce software, can create cybersecurity problems that closed-weight models often refuse to fix, because fixing a cybersecurity issue is very similar in practice to creating a cybersecurity issue (i.e. “white hat” hacking vs “black hat” hacking). There’s no way around this. When humans or bots write a lot of code, it comes with imperfections. And now, people are ironically turning to Chinese open-weight models to fix the bugs in their software, including ones created by American closed-weight models, since the American closed-weight models won’t fix them and the Chinese open-weight models will. The leading AI models are particularly good at exploiting bugs and creating cybersecurity problems, and the main way to defend against that is to have leading AI models stress-test your own software and fix the problems before the software is put into active use, and to regularly check them once they’re in use. I wrote about this back in 2023 when AI could barely write any usable code yet, and three short years later it’s starting to get there: Right now, at any given time, tons of hackers are trying to breach various software systems that we rely on, and some small percentage of them succeed, which results in a lot of data breaches and other issues. Now, imagine that a group of hackers or a government agency makes an AI that is optimized for hacking. In other words, some AI programs are optimized for beating humans in chess, and some AI programs can be optimized for hacking into systems better than humans can. Early chess AI learned from games between grandmaster human players, and then could beat those grandmasters every time. Recent chess AI instead learned from playing itself over and over, and then could beat those other AIs at chess. Now, suppose that a similar approach is used for hacking. In fact I would be surprised if multiple groups were not already working on this. So, first AI learns how to hack from absorbing existing techniques, and then graduates to learning how to hack from just iterating over and over at superhuman speed and rewriting its code to get better and better. Eventually it becomes orders of magnitude better at hacking than any human, and can breach any system that humans have designed. This could be open-sourced and broadly available. So what’s the defense against that? For systems that are connected to the internet and have a lot of complexity (and thus can’t realistically be made “unhackable” as some offline or basic systems can), the answer is more AI. Similar to how the only rivals to chess programs at chess are other chess programs, we’ll probably reach a point where the only defenses against AIs optimized for hacking are AIs optimized to update and defend software systems against being hacked. Imagine a world where superhuman hackers are always and everywhere trying to breach everything, and superhuman defenders are always and everywhere trying to prevent those breaches from happening. And both the attackers and defenders are constantly iterating and updating themselves as they learn from each other, while no human really knows what’s going on because the code is more complex than they can understand and is updated more quickly than they can keep up with. In that scenario, digital gods will be constantly battling each other in cyberspace in ways we can’t even comprehend, and yet the systems we all rely on are what’s at stake in that battle. -August 2023 Newsletter: Six AI Themes to Consider Calle, a physics PhD and open-source software developer, highlighted this problem recently in mid-July when he pointed out how he has to use Chinese AI to make his software secure: This got picked up by David Sacks, the President’s leading tech advisor: Shortly thereafter, Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, joined Twitter/X and made his first post about the importance of open-weight models: The next week, someone exploited a deficient random number generator in Coldcard bitcoin wallets and stole 1,300+ total coins from hundreds of users. Fiscal Cliff: Still Falling Extra fiscal spending pretty much ended at the end of July, and that’s a topic we’ve been covering in these reports for months. From April through July, people received stimulus checks and extra unemployment benefits, and small businesses received loans that turn into grants, nearly $3 trillion in free grant money overall, but most of that stopped by the end of July. Some of it happened with a lag; unemployment benefits attributed to previous weeks still went out to people into mid-August. Now, at the end of August, the economy has been operating for a couple weeks in “non-fiscal” mode. Unemployed people are not receiving additional federal unemployment benefits, and businesses are pretty much on their own. Small business revenue peaked in the beginning of July and has since been on a downtrend. July consumer confidence reached a new cycle low after enjoying a brief bounce. If this situation continues with high unemployment and low government stimulus, the natural results of a major recession will play out, with many people and businesses unable to pay rent, which trickles up to landlords and banks, and results in a broad solvency crisis and many defaults. So far, national personal income was up in 2020 (rather than down as in a normal recession), due to increased government transfer payments that more than offset the loss of normal income. And that led to retail sales also being up in 2020 (largely lead by e-commerce), because consumers have that government cash to spend, even as employment conditions, imports, exports, industrial production, and capital spending are all down as per what we’d expect from a severe recession. That divergence between incomes going up and economic activity going down is not inherently sustainable, unless government spending artificially continues to sustain it. Both political parties want another round of stimulus. The Republicans and President want about $1 trillion in stimulus, mainly targeting businesses and consumer stimulus checks again. The Democrats want $3 trillion in stimulus, targeting state budgets and larger consumer stimulus checks this time. Both sides have signaled compromise; Democrats are willing to go down to $2 trillion, and Trump is willing to go up to $1.3 trillion. Political events related to the upcoming election and unrelated to stimulus, largely involving the Post Office, have further slowed down these negotiations. The situation remains in gridlock, and so the economy has gone off the “fiscal cliff”. Analysts don’t expect S&P 500 earnings and revenue to surpass 2019 highs until 2022, even though the stock market has already reached new record highs in 2020, due to increases in valuation. As long as that fiscal gridlock remains, a disinflationary pressure and broad solvency risks grow. The Fed’s balance sheet stopped increasing nearly three months ago. Broad money supply stopped increasing about a month ago. The stock market and consumer finances are no longer held up by “money printing” at this particular time. Equities and other risk assets, which have kept going up, are vulnerable for correction in this environment. -August 30 deep dive report In essence, whenever the backdrop involves massive fiscal spending, rising inflation expectations, negative real interest rates that are becoming more deeply negative, and rapid increases in broad money supply; the logical move is to be in scarce assets. This includes things like precious metals, commodities, good-quality stocks, and Bitcoin, depending on your preferences. However, when the backdrop turns into gridlock and lack of fiscal stimulus, falling inflation expectations, rising real yields, and slower broad money supply growth, a more defensive position that includes cash and T-bills makes sense, potentially with hedges in place against drops in risk assets depending on what type of portfolio you run. We’re in a defense/disinflation environment until signs of stimulus emerge. On one hand they are getting a bit closer, with the Democrat-controlled House of Representative currently drafting a $2.4 trillion spending bill that is closer in size and scope to what the Republicans have said they would support. On the other side, the Republicans have moved up their target to $1.5 trillion, so the numbers are starting to converge towards the middle of maybe $2 trillion. The markets being in correction mode since their top on September 2nd certainly puts some added pressure on politicians, and particularly on Trump’s side, due to his frequent emphasis on stock market performance as a gauge of his success. There was less pressure for policymakers to do much as long as the stock market was going up and civil unrest was at bay, but now pressure is ratchetting up. However, the upcoming election and Supreme Court vacancy fight are potential detractors from getting a bipartisan stimulus deal done. I’ll leave the probability assessment of stimulus happening prior to the election to political specialists, and instead just watch the debate play out. Over the long run, more rounds of fiscal stimulus are nearly inevitable (as policymakers become pressured by struggling markets or heightened civil unrest), but between now and February, there’s a significant lack of policy clarity.

reference: Rate cuts could positively affect emerging markets by easing interest rates on dollar-denominated debts. This scenario is similar to the early 2000s when an easing dollar benefited these markets during a strong cycle from 2003-2007. Emerging market governments and companies might benefit as their debt burdens decrease, allowing them more financial flexibility. reference_contexts:
<1-hop>

Reserves as a % of GDP: Different countries have very different levels of foreign-exchange reserves when it comes to supporting their currency strength and backstopping external debt obligations when necessary. This is a more important metric for emerging markets but is relevant for all markets. Trade and trade balances as a % of GDP: Some countries are more reliant on exports/trade than other nations. And apart from that, some countries have trade surpluses while others have trade deficits, which is important when measuring how overvalued/undervalued a currency is and how competitive a market is on a global basis. Net International Investment Position as a % of GDP: A country that owns more foreign assets than foreigners own of their assets is a creditor nation (such as Japan). A country that owns fewer foreign assets than foreigners own of their assets is a debtor nation (such as the United States). For example, the United States and its citizens/firms (mainly its citizens/firms) own $29 trillion in foreign assets (stocks, bonds, and real estate), while foreigners own $40 trillion of U.S. assets, which gives the U.S. an -$11 trillion net international investment position, or about -52% of U.S. 2019 GDP. The United States became a creditor nation after World War I, meaning it owned more foreign assets than foreigners owned of its assets. However, by 1985, an accumulation of trade deficits left the United States to become a debtor nation. We kept consuming more than we produced, which means we sent dollars abroad each year and foreigners used those dollars to buy American assets. Meanwhile, Japan produced more than they consumed, so they accumulated dollars and other currencies, and used them to buy American assets and other foreign assets, which made them a creditor nation. During the 2008 crisis, the United States had a NIIP of about -10% of GDP. Since then, it has deteriorated to worse than -50% of GDP by 2019. It would require a current account surplus (and likely a weaker dollar relative to other currencies) to begin reversing that trend.
