The Precious Metal Divergence As I said in the previous report, volatility of this extreme level shakes the financial system down to its very foundations and tests securities across the board. In addition to stocks and corporate bonds selling off, safer havens like Treasury bonds and precious metals were hit this week, and several ETFs experienced record high dislocations, meaning that the difference between their market price and their net asset value (the sum value of all the stocks or assets they hold) reached a record large divide. For example, suppose there is an ETF that holds one share of Apple and one share of Amazon for each share of the ETF. You would expect the ETF’s efficient market price to be equal to the sum of Apple and Amazon’s share prices (which is the net asset value), or at least within a penny or so. Ninety-nine percent of the time, that’s the case. During extreme market events, however, with Apple and Amazon shares rising or falling by double-digit percentage points every day, that divide between market price and net asset value can widen. That’s the type of thing that happened to several ETFs this week, except the ETFs have dozens or hundreds of positions rather than just two as in this example. It appears that a number of risk parity funds had to unwind their positions. Risk parity funds invest in both stocks and bonds with heavy leverage. When stocks go down, bonds usually go up, which helps cushion the blow and keeps overall volatility low. This week, however, Treasury bond yields increased sharply, meaning that Treasury bond prices dropped sharply. The TLT 20+ year Treasury ETF, for example, dropped by nearly 15% from its sharp peak in just a few days: That’s not normal bond behavior. With Treasuries crashing so swiftly alongside stocks, leveraged funds holding stocks and bonds were in trouble and some probably liquidated, which results in indiscriminate selling. With yields going back up while there’s a deflationary crunch, it can put downward pressure on gold and silver temporarily as well. Late last week, and especially on Friday, gold, silver, platinum, and in particular palladium all sold off sharply. It was one of the record high volatility days for the whole metals complex. The move in the GDX gold miner’s ETF was particularly fascinating. It sold off so sharply on Thursday that it reached a -4% divergence from its net asset value, which was an all-time record. Then on Friday it broke that record by going to a -7% divergence from net asset value. Basically, there was so much indiscriminate selling pressure on GDX that market makers didn’t have time to arbitrage the discount to net asset value. This means that GDX’s market price closed Friday at over 7% below the sum value of the shares of gold miners it holds. President Trump gave a speech at around 3:30pm on Friday, where he declared a national emergency, which potentially opens the floodgates for federal bailout money to help states and businesses deal with the coronavirus shutdown. At the same time, gold miners went sharply down with ever-faster acceleration, before snapping furiously back up right into the final minutes of the trading day, and then were up sharply in after-hours trading. The last time that GDX had such a sharp sell-off was in 2008, shortly before it exploded higher. I don’t know what will happen going forward, but this has all the hallmarks of an indiscriminate selling liquidity crunch. Some big fund may have been long gold miners and short the S&P 500, and sharply unwound the position when the S&P 500 started to rally during the speech. Whatever exactly happened, something big liquidated or squeezed or broke. I bought some GDX right at the bottom there and updated it in real time in the Google Drive, but it all happened so fast, within minutes. What makes the sell-off in precious metals and miners even more interesting, was that at the same time it was happening, precious metal physical dealers were experiencing record physical metal buying. Large dealers like APMEX, JM Bullion, and many others put notices on their websites saying that due to extreme order volume, there would be long shipping delays, higher minimum orders, and so forth. user_input: How does Powell's approach to monetary policy reflect the challenges of managing inflation and financial stability in a high-debt environment?
reference: Powell's approach to monetary policy reflects significant challenges in managing inflation and financial stability within a high-debt context. The Federal Reserve, under Powell's leadership, has been combating fiscal-driven inflation reminiscent of the 1940s—characterized by high debts and monetary expansion primarily from fiscal deficits—with hawkish policies similar to those used in the 1970s when debts were lower and monetary expansion came mainly from bank lending. This strategy involves rapidly raising interest rates and reducing liquidity, which can lead to financial chaos given the current high debt levels. Powell faces a difficult decision: continue tightening monetary policy at the risk of damaging smaller banks and parts of the shadow banking system or pause and potentially allow inflation to rise. The situation is further complicated by ongoing bank crises and market volatility, making it challenging for the central bank to operate effectively in this 'long term debt cycle' environment.
reference_contexts:
<1-hop>

posted a number of times (with some new annotations this time), the Fed has been fighting 1940s-style fiscal-driven inflation (when debts are high and most of the monetary expansion is coming from fiscal deficits) with hawkish 1970s-style monetary policy (which works when debts are low and most of the monetary expansion is coming from bank lending). Raising rates that quickly and sucking liquidity out that quickly, when debts are still that high, leads to financial chaos. They now have a decision to either keep trying to tighten and damage the long-tail of small and medium banks and large swaths of the shadow banking system that they can’t even measure, or pause and risk letting inflation run hot. It’s rough for Powell because everyone is Monday-morning quarterbacking with these bank crises going on, and this type of “long term debt cycle” situation is the hardest environment for a central bank to operate in. Due to ongoing uncertainty and volatility, I continue to view a “three pillar portfolio” as the way to go for this decade, at least as a baseline. A classic 60/40 stock/bond portfolio benefits from disinflation, while this type of portfolio is more balanced, with significant protections against inflation. -The first pillar consists of high-quality profitable equities, with an emphasis on dividend-paying companies at reasonable valuations. Liquidity Indicators: Focusing on the Fed Although the Treasury’s refunding announcement was more important during these past couple weeks than the Fed’s decision and some of Powell’s speeches, the Fed news was still important. Fed Chairman Powell announced the Fed’s decision to pause interest rates for the moment. They implied to have no plans to cut them any time soon, and didn’t take future rate hikes off the table, but the overall remarks leaned somewhat dovish. He indicated that the sharp rise in long duration bond yields was doing some of his organization’s tightening for it, which gives the Fed more time to wait and assess incoming data. And then, during the week after that statement, bond yields fell by 20+ basis points, and undid some of the tightening that Powell had referred to. This ironically might make them lean toward staying hawkish, or at least trying to talk a bit more hawkishly in speeches to re-ignite some of the tightening. Senior loan officer surveys came out for Q4 2023, and across the board, they are easing up on their tightening of credit stands for the first time in a while: This survey checks with senior loan officers at banks to see if they are tightening lending standards or loosening them. The higher the number, the more that banks are actively tightening standards. If the number is negative, it means that on average they are loosening standards. This recent reading showed that 1) banks are still tightening standards but that 2) a smaller percentage of them are tightening than previously. In other words the rate-of-change is toward loosening, even as the absolute situation is still tightening. Does this tell us anything about the prospect for asset prices? Somewhat, yes. We have four prior recession points of data for this. The following chart shows the senior loan officer survey (inverted this time for visual clarity), vs the Wilshire 5000 total stock market index. -In 1990, the peak in credit tightening coincided with the market bottom. -In 2001, the peak in credit tightening occurred way before the market bottom; there was still plenty of price declines to go. This was a mild recession by most metrics, but the equity bubble had been bigger than normal and so it took a longer time to deflate and fell by a bigger percentage compared to a normal recession. -In 2008, the peak in credit tightening occurred a few months before the market bottom, when most of the drawdown was already finished. However, the real asset bubble this time was in real estate, and that didn’t bottom until early 2012. -In 2020, the peak in credit tightening occurred after the market had already bottomed and was heading back up. This was a very fast recession due to the unusual impact of the lockdowns and stimulus. Is there informational value to be derived from this relatively small three-decade dataset? Kind of. My takeaway is that when credit tightening starts to reverse a bit, that often marks the bottom or near-bottom of asset prices, except for when an asset class is in a particularly big bubble (like 2001 for equities or 2008 for housing). I continue to be less bearish than many of the bears, and less bullish than many of the bulls. Unusually large fiscal deficits create an atypical environment, and are stimulatory and inflationary for asset prices and the economy even as monetary policy is very restrictive toward real estate, junk-rated companies, and small businesses. There are two very powerful forces offsetting each other. I expect sideways choppy prices in many asset classes, within a very wide volatility band. If we look at CPI-adjusted equity prices, we can see that sometimes they take a long time to recover prior highs. It took nearly 20 years for CPI-adjusted equity prices to permanently surpass their early 1970s highs. It took about 15 years for CPI-adjusted equity prices to surpass their 2000 highs. How long will it take to surpass the 2021 highs? I would guess at least 5-10 years, but we’ll see.

user_input: How has the Treasury Department's strategy of 'activist Treasury issuance' influenced domestic liquidity conditions and interacted with Federal Reserve policies, particularly in terms of offsetting monetary tightening measures?
reference: The Treasury Department's strategy of 'activist Treasury issuance' (ATI) has significantly influenced domestic liquidity conditions by dynamically managing financial conditions through the adjustment of the maturity profile of its debt issuance. This approach involves issuing a higher ratio of short-duration T-bills, which are more 'money-like' and can be held similarly to cash due to their limited volatility. By doing so, the Treasury offsets some of the monetary tightening measures implemented by the Federal Reserve. Specifically, ATI has been used to counteract the Fed's balance sheet reduction efforts by increasing liquidity in the financial system through excess T-bill issuance. This strategy effectively reduces 10-year yields by roughly a quarter of a percent, providing economic stimulus comparable to a one-point cut in the Fed Funds rate. Consequently, ATI has neutralized the Fed's attempts to restrain the economy, contributing to persistent inflation and upward nominal growth surprises. If unwound, ATI could temporarily boost 10-year yields significantly, akin to a two-point hike in the Fed Funds rate.

Liquidity Check-Up US domestic liquidity and global liquidity conditions remain quite resilient despite the ongoing energy crisis. Back in December 2025, when bank reserve levels grew tight and domestic liquidity shortages were showing up, the Fed shifted from balance sheet reduction to gradual balance sheet expansion, to raise the aggregate level of reserves for banks on a structural basis. And specifically, the Fed determined that $20-$25 billion in monthly reserve creation was needed indefinitely, but purposely erred higher to $40 billion per month until tax day. This was to provide an extra liquidity buffer so that even when the April tax week liquidity suck occurs, banks would still have plenty of liquidity. And indeed, from Powell’s mid-December speech into mid-April, they averaged ::drumroll:: $41.5 billion in balance sheet growth per month over the span of four months. These were Fed chairman Powell’s remarks on the subject: As detailed in a statement released today by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, reserve management purchases will amount to $40 billion in the first month and may remain elevated for a few months to alleviate expected near-term pressures in money markets. Thereafter, we expect the size of reserve management purchases to decline, though the actual pace will depend on market conditions. […] So, you know, we announced that we’re resuming reserve management purchases. That is completely separate from monetary policy. It’s just we need to keep an ample supply of reserves out there. Why so big? The answer to that is, you know, if you look ahead, you will see that April 15th is coming up, and our framework is such that we want to have ample reserves even at times when reserves are at a low level temporarily. So that’s what happens on Tax Day. People pay a lot of money to the government, reserves drop sharply and temporarily. So this seasonal buildup that we’ll see in the next few months was going to happen anyway. It was going to happen because April 15th is April 15th. There’s also a secular ongoing growth of the balance sheet. We have to keep reserves, call it, constant as a—as it relates to the banking system or to the whole economy. And that alone calls for us to increase about $20 or $25 billion per month. -Jerome Powell, December 10th 2025 Press Conference Powell’s term as Fed chairman ends on May 15th, 2026. However, his term as a Fed governor goes until January 31, 2028 unless he elects to resign early (as outgoing chairmen often do) or is removed for cause. Kevin Warsh, who was previously on the Fed board, has been nominated by President Trump to be the next Fed chairman. He’s currently in the process of going through the Senate confirmation. Warsh has advocated for a smaller Fed balance sheet, but he’s unlikely to achieve that at scale, and if he does, it’ll mainly be in a liquidity-neutral way. I outlined the reasons and scenarios for that in my February 2026 public newsletter: Below-Baseline Scenarios President Trump has announced that his nominee for the next Fed chairman (a term that starts in May 2026) will be Kevin Warsh. The U.S. Senate would have to confirm it at that time to make it official. Warsh is on record saying he is in favor of a smaller Fed balance sheet, which is in contrast to the Fed’s existing forecasts. Therefore, it needs to be asked: could a shake-up in leadership at the Fed change their balance sheet composition? The answer is likely “not much” but with some caveats. -The chairman is powerful, but he’s only one of 12 votes on the Federal Open Market Committee, so he doesn’t unilaterally set policy. -The Fed and other federal agencies could further ease bank regulations, allowing them to hold more treasuries without negatively impacting their regulatory leverage ratios. That means the Fed can own fewer treasuries. -The Fed could take some steps to discourage excess reserve accumulation at banks, thereby distributing the reserves that are in the system a bit more evenly. This could let them shrink their balance sheet by perhaps a few hundred billion dollars. -The Treasury Department could increase its average debt duration and shrink its average cash account size (known as the Treasury General Account). A smaller cash account size would give more liquidity back to the banking system, enabling a smaller Fed balance sheet by perhaps a few hundred billion dollars. However, the government generally doesn’t want higher long-term interest rates, so they’re sensitive about how much supply of long-duration debt they issue. In theory, if all of those things were done, the Fed’s balance sheet could go down by somewhere around a trillion dollars. However, the chances of that happening are low. And importantly, all of those measures just move liquidity around. Banks buying more treasuries on fractional reserve is functionally similar to the Fed buying them with new reserves. And moving reserves around and reducing the Treasury General Account basically result in efficiency gains: doing more with less. At the end of the day, the Fed is going to optimize for 1) maintaining bank lending and broad money creation at a moderate pace, 2) ensuring the treasury security market remains liquid, and 3) ensuring that the repo market remains liquid and that any liquidity stresses that do pop up don’t remain acute for very long. -Lyn Alden, February 8th 2026 newsletter Current usage of the Fed’s standing repo facility remains muted, and the SOFR-IORB spread is fine as well, which together suggest that domestic liquidity conditions are fine at the moment. Looking globally, the dollar index remains choppy, and there aren’t really any signs of an acute global liquidity shortage. Last week, multiple nations including the UAE that were hard-hit by this war on Iran asked for swap lines with the United States, and many people on social media took that as a sign of acute dollar shortage liquidity problems. Macro View Liquidity Indicators Domestic liquidity indicators continue to run almost perfectly sideways, in large part because the Treasury and Fed have been in lockstep regarding this: Notably, Stephen Miran and Nouriel Roubini recently published a paper about “Activist Treasury Issuance” which is their term that refers to the Treasury Department taking unusual actions to offset the Fed’s tightness. Both Miran and Roubini are economics PhDs and worked in various capacities with the Treasury Department in the past. In the paper, they argued that the Treasury has been shortening the average duration of its debt issuance via excess T-bill issuance, and thus offsetting some of the monetary tightening that the Fed has been doing. It’s normal for the Treasury to issue an excessive ratio of T-bills during a crisis such as in 2020, but it’s highly unusual for them to be doing it in relatively benign economic and market conditions like we’ve had over the past couple years. I’d argue that it’s a symptom of the ongoing fiscal dominance that the United States finds itself in. T-bills are more “money-like” than longer duration T-bonds, and so when a government finds itself issuing a ton of debt at a time when neither their central bank nor their primary foreign investors are currently buying that issuance, they can issue more short-duration debt. Short duration debt, being of limited volatility, can be held by investors similar to how they would hold cash. Here’s Miran and Roubini’s executive summary: By adjusting the maturity profile of its debt issuance, Treasury is dynamically managing financial conditions and through them, the economy, usurping core functions of the Federal Reserve. We dub this novel tool “activist Treasury issuance,” or ATI. By manipulating the amount of interest rate risk owned by investors, ATI works through the same channels as the Fed’s quantitative easing programs. ATI has been a major market driver over the past year and we expect it will continue to play a significant role in the years ahead; ATI may become a regular element of the policy toolbox, driving political business cycles in the market and the economy. We calculate that ATI has reduced 10-year yields over the last year by roughly a quarter of a percent, providing similar stimulus as a one-point cut in the Fed Funds rate, the central bank’s primary policy tool. Combined with higher neutral rates, ATI implies the total stance of both monetary and issuance policy, considered together, is roughly neutral—in other words, ATI has interdicted the Fed’s attempt to restrain the economy, helping explain inflation persistence and upward nominal growth surprises over the past year. If ATI is unwound via terming out $1 trillion of excess Treasury Bills, we expect it to temporarily boost 10-year yields by 50 basis points, before settling into a permanent 30-bp increase, with corresponding price changes in risk assets. A 50-bp increase in the 10-year yield will have similar economic effects as a two-point hike in the Fed Funds rate. If ATI is not unwound but becomes a permanently employed policy tool, we are likely to see higher equilibrium inflation and interest rates priced in over time due to political business cycles becoming reality. Regular readers of my work will be quite familiar with this concept. I start most of my reports by discussing liquidity conditions, including what the Treasury has been doing with its excess T-bill issuance. And at the start of this year, I dedicated my January 2024 newsletter to this phenomenon of the Treasury offsetting the Fed. Here was a key snippet: Ever since the fourth quarter of 2022, and extending all throughout 2023, the U.S. Federal Reserve and the U.S. Treasury have been operating opposite policies from each other. And the Treasury has had to pull two different levers to keep up with the Fed. -From September 2022 through May 2023, the Treasury drained their own cash reserves back into the financial system, which offset the Fed. -From June 2023 to the present, the Treasury rapidly increased their T-bill issuance as a percentage of their debt issuance and thus drained reverse repos back into the financial system, which offset the Fed. This following chart shows the Fed vs Treasury liquidity actions in year-over-year change terms. For this chart, higher means more liquidity, and lower means less liquidity. The Fed in blue has been doing its part to reduce liquidity in the financial system since early 2022. The Treasury in red (reflecting both their own cash balances and their ability to affect the reverse repo facility based on their ability to issue T-bills) has been doing its part to increase liquidity in the financial system since late 2022. The net result is that domestic liquidity was decreasing until Q4 2022 but then began to flatten out and turn slightly upward when the Treasury began its inverse operation: -January 2024 Newsletter, “Fiscal and Monetary Divergence While I’m more focused on the liquidity impacts, Miran and Roubini’s paper attempts to quantify the effect by comparing it to interest rate changes. They argue that the Treasury’s excessive T-bill issuance has been the equivalent of the Fed cutting interest rates by 1%. And they argue that if this were to be unwound, it would temporarily be similar to a 2% rate hike by the Fed. I don’t have any particular view regarding if their interest rate comparison is accurate or not, but in my view it’s less about rates per se, and more about liquidity and smooth financial plumbing, of which rates are only a part. Meanwhile, global liquidity is rangebound, but I continue to have a view that it’ll likely grind higher over the next 18 months. If we get some of the capital rotations discussed later in this report, then that could be a catalyst for such a move higher, which can feed on itself. I don’t have any firm conviction for the next quarter.

user_input: How has the Treasury Department's strategy of increasing T-bill issuance impacted domestic liquidity and monetary policy effectiveness?
reference: The Treasury Department's strategy of increasing T-bill issuance has significantly impacted domestic liquidity by improving it, as short-duration T-bills meet excess demand that was previously held in the reverse repo facility. This action draws money out of the reverse repo facility into holding T-bills, thereby injecting liquidity back into the financial system. The increased issuance of T-bills helps offset the Federal Reserve's quantitative tightening (balance sheet reduction), creating a neutral domestic liquidity environment. However, this strategy has also affected monetary policy effectiveness by usurping some core functions traditionally managed by the Federal Reserve. By adjusting the maturity profile of its debt issuance, the Treasury is dynamically managing financial conditions and influencing economic outcomes, similar to how the Fed's quantitative easing programs work. This 'activist Treasury issuance' (ATI) has been a major market driver, reducing 10-year yields by roughly a quarter of a percent over the past year, providing stimulus akin to a one-point cut in the Fed Funds rate. If unwound, ATI could temporarily boost 10-year yields significantly, similar to a two-point hike in the Fed Funds rate.
reference_contexts:
<1-hop>

Liquidity Indicators: Focusing on the Treasury Domestic liquidity in the United States continues to be almost perfectly flat, and is likely what policymakers are managing for. The Treasury Department surprised market participants with their quarterly refunding announcement by substantially raising the percentage of upcoming debt issuance that will be done with T-bills. In a sign of fiscal dominance, this is probably the first time where a Treasury refunding announcement was more important for markets than a Fed FOMC policy update. This is all kind of wonky but can be simplified as follows. A healthy sovereign bond market has plenty of liquidity (i.e. good trading volumes where even a large entity can buy or sell a ton of bonds without moving the price noticeably), and no problem issuing a sizable percentage of long duration bonds. However, the U.S. sovereign bond market is not very healthy due to such large ongoing deficits combined with the Fed’s ongoing balance sheet reduction. So, yields keep rising and are very volatile, bond liquidity is low, and small banks are being squeezed in the process. So, the Treasury decided to increase its issuance of short-duration T-bills for its upcoming deficit issuance beyond its normal T-bill ratio. This improves liquidity conditions, but around the margins is the kind of thing that emerging markets do when facing debt and currency problems. The big pool of remaining liquidity available to buy Treasuries is the money that is still stuck in the reverse repo facility. All of this reverse repo money basically represents excess T-bill demand, and the Fed maintains the reserve repo facility so that the market doesn’t drive T-bill yields below the lower floor of their interest rate target. In contrast, there isn’t much demand for longer-duration bonds. And so as the Treasury issues more and more T-bills, it helps meet that excess T-bill demand that exists, and money starts to come out of the reverse repo facility and into holding T-bills. The Treasury then spends this money back into the economy and financial system. The reverse repo facility is now under $1 trillion for the first time since 2021: The ongoing drawdown of the reverse repo facility is putting liquidity back into the system, and how fast it is drained partially depends on how many T-bills the Treasury issues as a ratio of their total debt issuance. By increasing T-bill issuance, they continue to draw money out of the reverse repo facility. And at the current pace, it almost exactly offsets the Fed’s ongoing quantitative tightening (balance sheet reduction), to create a neutral domestic liquidity environment. Once it runs out, liquidity problems could become pretty severe and require a change of course by the Fed. Why is this important? The reason is because the U.S. is facing a slow-moving fiscal crisis for the first time in decades. We’re running 7%-of-GDP deficits despite unemployment rates being very low, and since we are no longer in an environment of structurally falling interest rates, interest expense is starting to become a problem for the first time in decades. And that chart somewhat understates the issue. At $34 trillion in debt, and if interest rates just stay where they are, then as more and more public debt matures and gets refinanced at these higher rates, it will approach $1.7 trillion in annual interest expense, or 6% of GDP (a record high). A recession that forces the Fed to cut interest rates would alleviate some of the interest expense, but usually in recessions fiscal deficits rise sharply because tax revenue drops. For most metrics, I prefer looking at figures relative to GDP or other proportional items, but I think looking at the absolute dollar amount of fiscal deficits is important for one key reason: large fiscal deficits can be inflationary and fuel nominal GDP growth. Analysts who only look at the deficit as a percentage of GDP will likely continue to be surprised by the sheer scale of the deficits and the sheer growth of nominal GDP.

<2-hop>

Macro View Liquidity Indicators Domestic liquidity indicators continue to run almost perfectly sideways, in large part because the Treasury and Fed have been in lockstep regarding this: Notably, Stephen Miran and Nouriel Roubini recently published a paper about “Activist Treasury Issuance” which is their term that refers to the Treasury Department taking unusual actions to offset the Fed’s tightness. Both Miran and Roubini are economics PhDs and worked in various capacities with the Treasury Department in the past. In the paper, they argued that the Treasury has been shortening the average duration of its debt issuance via excess T-bill issuance, and thus offsetting some of the monetary tightening that the Fed has been doing. It’s normal for the Treasury to issue an excessive ratio of T-bills during a crisis such as in 2020, but it’s highly unusual for them to be doing it in relatively benign economic and market conditions like we’ve had over the past couple years. I’d argue that it’s a symptom of the ongoing fiscal dominance that the United States finds itself in. T-bills are more “money-like” than longer duration T-bonds, and so when a government finds itself issuing a ton of debt at a time when neither their central bank nor their primary foreign investors are currently buying that issuance, they can issue more short-duration debt. Short duration debt, being of limited volatility, can be held by investors similar to how they would hold cash. Here’s Miran and Roubini’s executive summary: By adjusting the maturity profile of its debt issuance, Treasury is dynamically managing financial conditions and through them, the economy, usurping core functions of the Federal Reserve. We dub this novel tool “activist Treasury issuance,” or ATI. By manipulating the amount of interest rate risk owned by investors, ATI works through the same channels as the Fed’s quantitative easing programs. ATI has been a major market driver over the past year and we expect it will continue to play a significant role in the years ahead; ATI may become a regular element of the policy toolbox, driving political business cycles in the market and the economy. We calculate that ATI has reduced 10-year yields over the last year by roughly a quarter of a percent, providing similar stimulus as a one-point cut in the Fed Funds rate, the central bank’s primary policy tool. Combined with higher neutral rates, ATI implies the total stance of both monetary and issuance policy, considered together, is roughly neutral—in other words, ATI has interdicted the Fed’s attempt to restrain the economy, helping explain inflation persistence and upward nominal growth surprises over the past year. If ATI is unwound via terming out $1 trillion of excess Treasury Bills, we expect it to temporarily boost 10-year yields by 50 basis points, before settling into a permanent 30-bp increase, with corresponding price changes in risk assets. A 50-bp increase in the 10-year yield will have similar economic effects as a two-point hike in the Fed Funds rate. If ATI is not unwound but becomes a permanently employed policy tool, we are likely to see higher equilibrium inflation and interest rates priced in over time due to political business cycles becoming reality. Regular readers of my work will be quite familiar with this concept. I start most of my reports by discussing liquidity conditions, including what the Treasury has been doing with its excess T-bill issuance. And at the start of this year, I dedicated my January 2024 newsletter to this phenomenon of the Treasury offsetting the Fed. Here was a key snippet: Ever since the fourth quarter of 2022, and extending all throughout 2023, the U.S. Federal Reserve and the U.S. Treasury have been operating opposite policies from each other. And the Treasury has had to pull two different levers to keep up with the Fed. -From September 2022 through May 2023, the Treasury drained their own cash reserves back into the financial system, which offset the Fed. -From June 2023 to the present, the Treasury rapidly increased their T-bill issuance as a percentage of their debt issuance and thus drained reverse repos back into the financial system, which offset the Fed. This following chart shows the Fed vs Treasury liquidity actions in year-over-year change terms. For this chart, higher means more liquidity, and lower means less liquidity. The Fed in blue has been doing its part to reduce liquidity in the financial system since early 2022. The Treasury in red (reflecting both their own cash balances and their ability to affect the reverse repo facility based on their ability to issue T-bills) has been doing its part to increase liquidity in the financial system since late 2022. The net result is that domestic liquidity was decreasing until Q4 2022 but then began to flatten out and turn slightly upward when the Treasury began its inverse operation: -January 2024 Newsletter, “Fiscal and Monetary Divergence While I’m more focused on the liquidity impacts, Miran and Roubini’s paper attempts to quantify the effect by comparing it to interest rate changes. They argue that the Treasury’s excessive T-bill issuance has been the equivalent of the Fed cutting interest rates by 1%. And they argue that if this were to be unwound, it would temporarily be similar to a 2% rate hike by the Fed. I don’t have any particular view regarding if their interest rate comparison is accurate or not, but in my view it’s less about rates per se, and more about liquidity and smooth financial plumbing, of which rates are only a part. Meanwhile, global liquidity is rangebound, but I continue to have a view that it’ll likely grind higher over the next 18 months. If we get some of the capital rotations discussed later in this report, then that could be a catalyst for such a move higher, which can feed on itself. I don’t have any firm conviction for the next quarter.

user_input: How does Cheesecake Factory Inc's acquisition of Fox Restaurant Concepts (FRC) align with its long-term growth strategy, and what are the expected impacts on revenue growth and valuation?
reference: Cheesecake Factory Inc's acquisition of Fox Restaurant Concepts (FRC) is a strategic move to enhance its long-term growth potential. The company aims to leverage FRC's successful restaurant concepts like North Italia and Flower Child as new growth drivers, complementing the mature cash-generating brand of Cheesecake Factory itself. This acquisition brings diversification and significant growth opportunities, with plans to scale North Italia from 21 locations to about 200 in the United States. The company expects these newer brands to drive substantial revenue growth, targeting a 20% annual increase in location count for North Italia and other FRC concepts, compared to a more modest 3% growth rate for The Cheesecake Factory locations. This strategy is expected to accelerate overall revenue growth from historical rates of 3.7% over the past five years to an estimated 6% going forward. In terms of valuation, while Cheesecake Factory Inc's stock is not considered 'cheap' by most measures, it is viewed as appropriately valued given its stronger balance sheet and performance compared to other restaurant chains. The acquisition supports this valuation by providing a realistic path for increased growth rates through the expansion of high-margin concepts like North Italia, which boasts a 35% cash-on-cash return potential per location.

And here are their P/S and P/B ratios since inception: Chart Source: Y Charts 1-year earnings growth: 9.9% 3-year annualized earnings growth: -1.9% 5-year annualized earnings growth: 6.3% 10-year annualized earnings growth: 9.6% 15-year annualized earnings growth: 7.7% Analysts on average currently expect 7.4% annualized earnings growth during the two years from the end of 2019 through the end of 2021. The company targets 13-14% annual returns going forward with their current post-acquisition structure, based on this breakdown: Source: Cheesecake Factory October 2019 Presentation I’m going to go ahead and just downgrade their revenue growth estimate from 8% to 6% right from the start for valuation purposes. The company grew revenue at a 3.7% annualized rate over the past five years and an 4.0% annualized rate over the past ten years. Granted, the company now has more aggressive growth drivers post-acquisition, and they expect The Cheesecake Factory to drive about half of the growth in line with their historical figures (3-4%) while North Italia and FRC are expected to drive the other half of growth with a faster pace from their much smaller base, which gives a credible reason to believe in upcoming growth acceleration. However, I’ll believe 8% when I see it. That’s double their 5-year and 10-year growth rates. For now, let’s conservatively say about 6% growth going forward based on significant contribution from these new opportunities. I’d rather be happily surprised to the upside rather than disappointed to the downside. Next, the company factors in a 2.5% dividend yield, but due to lower valuations currently, it’s more like 3.3%. That’s not bad, compared to the S&P 500 average yield of around 1.8% these days. Lastly, the company expects to reduce its share count by 1.5% per year, and to pay down acquisition debt over time even though its balance sheet remains in solid shape. Total capital returns from dividends, buybacks, and debt reduction are expected to average 5.5% per year. With $2.65 expected EPS for the full-year 2019, this is my base case valuation model: At the current price of $43.22, this stock is reasonably valued for 10% expected long-term returns without factoring in valuation expansion, which I believe is better than the S&P 500 is prepared to deliver from current valuation levels. In addition, with a strong balance sheet, good management, and a proven business model, it’s not very risky, as long as it is part of a diversified portfolio. With a more bullish scenario of 8% growth and eventually selling the stock for a higher earnings multiple of 18, 13-14% long-term returns are indeed possible from today’s price point, but I would not use that as my base case. That’s the optimistic case. Margin improvement from North Italia‘s growth could also give a performance boost. The base case is pretty good, the downside risks are real but well-managed in my view, and the upside potential is very significant. Basically, this is an example of a stock that transitioned from a high-valuation growth stock into a more mature dividend-paying quality/value stock with a more modest growth rate. However, with the acquisition of FRC and the company’s plan to scale North Italia nationwide, the company has a realistic path to increase their growth rate again. Risks Industry Competition- Moderate Risk The primary risk for any restaurant stock is that it ceases to have the most relevant food and environment for changing consumer preferences. The restaurant industry is one of the most challenging, and it requires good management to keep a tight ship and to continually update the menu and environment in order to maintain strong customer traffic. The company updates their menu twice per year, including pricing changes, and in response to criticism about their large portion sizes, The Cheesecake Factory has introduced what they refer to as a SkinnyLicious menu subset that focuses on lower-calorie portions. With Cheesecake Factory Inc’s strong management team, and with the added diversification of North Italia and other brands within Fox Restaurant Concepts, I believe that the company is well-protected from some of the more negative scenarios that restaurants can face. However, it’s always a risk worth monitoring. Margin Pressure- Major Risk Cheesecake Factory’s international licensed locations offer high margins, but their company-operated locations, which represent the bulk of their revenue, have been under margin pressure. Labor costs have been increasing but the company has been slow to raise menu prices. Operating margins reached a peak of 8.8% in 2016 but are currently as low as 5.9%. The growth of North Italia, with its significant alcohol mix leading to 35% cash-on-cash return potential per location, may help to offset these margin pressures as that chain becomes a larger portion of the overall company. Executive Retention- Moderate Risk As previously described, Cheesecake Factory Inc has been well-managed by its co-founder, David Overton, since 1992. He is currently 73, which means he could potentially have a decade or more leading the company ahead of him, or could retire at any time. The company has a strong executive team with long tenures at the company, but losing a co-founder as its long-time CEO would bring about transition risk. Specifically, there’s always a risk with new non-founder management that the company could lose its long-term focus and become more “corporate” with an increased focus on quarterly results and executive compensation, rather than focusing on the long-term process of building a successful company as they have been doing. On the flip side, fresh management at the top might help the company boost margins. For example, they might decide to streamline The Cheesecake Factory’s massive menu, which it seems to me

the late 1970’s, her son David Overton started opening small The Cheesecake Factory restaurants, and incorporated the chain into a company in 1992. David Overton remains the CEO to this day, and has successfully led the company with a long-term focus since its inception. Many other top executives at the company have long tenures as well. This isn’t a company that focuses on short-term quarterly results, and instead clearly focuses on long-term profitable performance and retaining their management hierarchy for long tenures. Multiple studies show that mature/profitable companies that focus on earning high returns on invested capital (ROIC) statistically do quite well, and Overton’s company specifically looks to earn an average ROIC of over 15% per year, which they often achieve. This is evidence of a well-run operation, but with natural periods of weakness that align with recessions. Chart Source: Y Charts The Cheesecake Factory has a 3.7 out of 5 rating on Glassdoor.com, which puts it higher than most other large restaurant chains for employee satisfaction. P.F. Chang’s has a 3.3 rating, Chili’s has 3.4, Olive Garden has 3.5, and Outback Steakhouse has 3.6. A few companies have higher ratings, like Longhorn Steakhouse has 3.9, and privately-owned In-N-Out Burger has an astoundingly high 4.3. Fox Restaurant Concepts, which is now a subsidiary of the company, also has an unusually high rating of 4.1. Cheesecake Factory Inc has also been rated as one of Fortune’s Top 100 employers for the past six years in a row. The company has historically maintained little or no long term debt, which gives them exceptional balance sheet strength for a small company. During the most recent quarter, however, they borrowed approximately $300 million in debt in order to finance the acquisition of FRC, and they plan to gradually pay this down. Even with this increased leverage, they only have a debt/income ratio of about 2-3x. In comparison, Bloomin Brands (the parent company of Outback Steakhouse) has a debt/income ratio of over 8x, which is very high. They trade at lower valuations than Cheesecake Factory Inc but have a lot less balance sheet flexibility. Growth Plans and FRC Acquisition There was a small company called Fox Restaurant Concepts (“FRC” for short), founded by Sam Fox in 1998, that serves as an incubator/developer for new restaurant concepts. Sam Fox has developed a highly successful record of building out restaurant ideas and selling some of the mature ones to other funds or businesses. In 2016, Cheesecake Factory Inc invested into two of Fox’s mature restaurant concepts, North Italia and Flower Child. Recently, after this multi-year period of successful co-investment, the company was in talks to purchase those mature restaurant chains from Fox. However, they decided to go a step further, and in July 2019, they announced an agreement to acquire all of Fox Restaurant Concepts. They now own North Italia, Flower Child, and a variety of smaller concepts, as well as the incubator structure itself. Sam Fox will continue to lead FRC as an independent subsidiary of Cheesecake Factory Inc, operating as a restaurant concept incubator. North Italia operations will move from FRC’s HQ in Arizona to the Cheesecake Factory’s HQ in California, so that the company can begin scaling that chain up alongside The Cheesecake Factory. The rest of the smaller concepts will continue to be led by FRC in Arizona, with the option to scale the mature ones up over time as they become mature and proven enough. North Italia currently has 21 locations, and Cheesecake Factory Inc expects that they can scale the chain to about 200 in the United States. They have a streamlined Italian upscale casual menu with an extensive wine and cocktail selection, and alcohol sales account for over 30% of total sales (compared to only 12% for The Cheesecake Factory restaurants). Private dining is a more significant portion of their sales than most restaurant chains. These locations are very profitable, with a 35% cash-on-cash return according to the company. The company expects to increase the location count of The Cheesecake Factory by about 3% per year, while North Italia and various FRC locations are expected to increase by 20% per year or more. The company’s namesake brand is the mature cash-generator, while these other concepts are the growth drivers. I think this acquisition has great synergy. FRC and their North Italia brand bring diversification and significant growth potential. Cheesecake Factory Inc brings plenty of capital for more rapid expansion of Fox’s mature restaurant concepts, and provides logistics and other operational infrastructure to scale them up as well. Valuation Analysis Cheesecake Factory Inc’s stock is not “cheap” by most measures, but it is appropriately-valued in my view at a time when many stocks are overvalued. It has a better balance sheet and stronger performance than many other restaurant chains, which affords it a higher valuation by the market. However, it is currently at-or-below its historical average valuation levels based on most time periods due to a recent bout of weakness. The stock currently has a dividend yield of over 3.3%, and has grown the dividend each year since they started paying it in 2012. user_input: How has the US dollar's performance been influenced by economic factors such as fiscal deficits and money supply growth?
reference: The US dollar experienced weakness over the past year due to several economic factors. The United States ran the largest fiscal deficits as a percentage of GDP, which contributed significantly to its broad money (M2) supply growing at an approximately 24% annualized rate from October 2019 through October 2020. This growth in money supply was partly driven by the US Federal Reserve being the largest buyer of Treasury debt issuance needed to fund these deficits. The combination of large fiscal deficits and rapid expansion of the money supply has been a key factor influencing the dollar's performance, leading it to break below lower-bound support levels established earlier in the year and reach multi-year lows against a basket of other major currencies.

Meanwhile, commodities, equities, and nominal Treasury yields are currently corroborating the higher-inflation theme over the past month. Dollar Update Over the past month, the dollar broke below the lower-bound support levels that it established this summer, and reached multi-year lows in reference to a basket of other major currencies. Here’s the dollar index chart: My research piece on the global reserve system goes into detail on the US dollar. And as I explain in that article, I have no strong opinion about the next 3-6 months for the dollar (economic shutdowns and fiscal stimulus levels both factor heavily into that period), but I remain longer-term dollar bearish. The next support level for the dollar index is just below 89. This was the low from early 2018. Similarly, the EUR/USD pair (and the euro is the biggest component of the dollar index comparison basket) has a resistance level at $1.25 dollars to per euro. Broad money (M2) growth from October 2019 through October 2020: Euro Area: 10% Japan: 8% United States: 24% China: 10% So, it’s not too shocking that the dollar had some weakness this year. A lot of folks look at economic growth or economic indicators without considering what it took to get those numbers. Both pre-pandemic and post-pandemic, the US is juicing its economy much more than others with large fiscal deficits, and since late 2019, the US Federal Reserve is the largest buyer of the Treasury debt issuance to fund those deficits. Ultimately I sided with the pro argument, saying that due to the structural changes happening with developed market fiscal environments and a globally shifting central bank policy of leaning a bit more into gold, that’s the side I want to err on despite the frothiness: The good news lately is that gold is back to the top end of that consolidation range, and has touched above the psychologically important $3,500/oz range. That’s why since autumn 2018 when I added precious metals to the newsletter portfolio, I’ve happily erred on staying long even through periods where I expect intermediate-term weakness. Money Metals visualizes it well in their quarterly newsletter. The dollar is no longer expanding as a share of global reserves, and gold is no longer falling, in what is likely the bottom of a trend that basically began after WWII: After all these 5 months of price chop, I am increasingly uncertain as to whether to expect a breakout or more consolidation. user_input: How does Darden Restaurants' financial strategy during a recession compare to Cheesecake Factory Inc's approach, particularly in terms of liquidity and debt management?
reference: Darden Restaurants and Cheesecake Factory Inc both have strategies to manage financial challenges during a recession, focusing on liquidity and debt management. Darden has about $800 million in net debt with a debt/income ratio slightly above 1. They face potential issues with their $4+ billion in capital leases but can draw from an unused $750 million revolving credit facility for liquidity. Their accounts payable stand at $340 million, while they have $157 million in cash on hand. In contrast, Cheesecake Factory Inc has historically maintained little or no long-term debt, providing them with strong balance sheet flexibility. However, during the most recent quarter, they borrowed approximately $300 million to finance an acquisition, resulting in a debt/income ratio of about 2-3x. Despite this increased leverage, their financial strategy still allows for significant growth potential and operational expansion.

With about $800 million in net debt, their debt/income ratio is only a little bit above 1. Their $4+ billion in capital leases could be an issue, even though it wouldn’t be an issue in a normal recession. Federal measures to provide temporary relief for businesses and workers in the hospitality/tourism/restaurant/airline sectors may further help soften the blow, but things like that are unclear at the moment. A problem is that Darden entered this quarter with $340 million in accounts payable and just $157 million in cash on hand. However, they have an unused $750 million revolving credit facility that they can draw from, for problems just like this. So, they should have plenty of liquidity for a couple terrible quarters. Although the company recently launched paid sick leave (1 hour of sick leave for every 30 hours worked), they’ll also inevitably cut a lot of their labor costs. Restaurant expenses may decrease a bit but some are fixed. Interest payments are fixed, but small each quarter. Depreciation and amortization are non-cash items. So there is a lot of flexibility here, even though they’ll take a big hit if this goes on for more than a quarter. Conservative investors should probably wait for some signs of slowdown in the coronavirus spread here in the United States and talk of re-opening things before investing in something like Darden. By then, the bottom for the stock may very well be in, but there will be less downside risk. Aggressive investors may find it interesting to start forming a small position within the context of a well-diversified portfolio, if you start with the assumption that by the end of this, most restaurants won’t be bankrupt. Growth Plans and FRC Acquisition There was a small company called Fox Restaurant Concepts (“FRC” for short), founded by Sam Fox in 1998, that serves as an incubator/developer for new restaurant concepts. Sam Fox has developed a highly successful record of building out restaurant ideas and selling some of the mature ones to other funds or businesses. In 2016, Cheesecake Factory Inc invested into two of Fox’s mature restaurant concepts, North Italia and Flower Child. Recently, after this multi-year period of successful co-investment, the company was in talks to purchase those mature restaurant chains from Fox. However, they decided to go a step further, and in July 2019, they announced an agreement to acquire all of Fox Restaurant Concepts. They now own North Italia, Flower Child, and a variety of smaller concepts, as well as the incubator structure itself. Sam Fox will continue to lead FRC as an independent subsidiary of Cheesecake Factory Inc, operating as a restaurant concept incubator. North Italia operations will move from FRC’s HQ in Arizona to the Cheesecake Factory’s HQ in California, so that the company can begin scaling that chain up alongside The Cheesecake Factory. The rest of the smaller concepts will continue to be led by FRC in Arizona, with the option to scale the mature ones up over time as they become mature and proven enough. North Italia currently has 21 locations, and Cheesecake Factory Inc expects that they can scale the chain to about 200 in the United States. They have a streamlined Italian upscale casual menu with an extensive wine and cocktail selection, and alcohol sales account for over 30% of total sales (compared to only 12% for The Cheesecake Factory restaurants). Private dining is a more significant portion of their sales than most restaurant chains. These locations are very profitable, with a 35% cash-on-cash return according to the company. The company expects to increase the location count of The Cheesecake Factory by about 3% per year, while North Italia and various FRC locations are expected to increase by 20% per year or more. The company’s namesake brand is the mature cash-generator, while these other concepts are the growth drivers. I think this acquisition has great synergy. FRC and their North Italia brand bring diversification and significant growth potential. Cheesecake Factory Inc brings plenty of capital for more rapid expansion of Fox’s mature restaurant concepts, and provides logistics and other operational infrastructure to scale them up as well.
